overview:
France in the late 1780s was not a poor country, but its monarchy was insolvent. Decades of war — including bankrolling the American revolutionaries — had loaded the crown with debt it could not service, and the tax system's central absurdity was that the clergy and nobility, the people best able to pay, were largely exempt from paying. Attempts at reform ran into entrenched resistance; when the parlement of Grenoble was ordered dissolved in June 1788, townspeople pelted the troops from the rooftops in the Day of the Tiles, one of the moments some historians treat as the Revolution's true opening. Louis XVI finally summoned the Estates General in May 1789, the first meeting since 1614. The Third Estate refused to be outvoted by the other two, declared itself a National Assembly, and on 14 July a Paris crowd hunting gunpowder stormed the Bastille — a fortress holding only a handful of prisoners, but a perfect symbol of arbitrary royal power. Within weeks the Assembly had abolished feudal privilege and issued the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen.

What followed was not a single revolution but a chain of them, each overtaking the last. A constitutional monarchy was attempted and failed: the king's flight toward the frontier in June 1791 destroyed what trust remained, and a month later the National Guard fired on a republican petition on the Champ de Mars. The same summer, in the papal enclave of Avignon, revolutionary partisans butchered dozens of prisoners in the massacres of La Glacière — an early sign of how localized and vicious the violence could get. War with Austria from April 1792 fused foreign invasion to domestic paranoia. The insurrection of 10 August 1792 overthrew the monarchy outright; three weeks later, with Prussian armies advancing, Paris crowds emptied the prisons in the September Massacres, killing somewhere between roughly 1,100 and 1,600 people, most of them ordinary criminals rather than political prisoners. The Republic was proclaimed, Louis XVI guillotined in January 1793, and the Terror followed — near 17,000 formal executions and tens of thousands more deaths in prison and in the civil war in the Vendée, alongside frontier sieges like Maubeuge that held the invading coalition at bay. The Revolution also reached across the Atlantic: pressed by the slave uprising in Saint-Domingue, the Convention abolished slavery in all French colonies in February 1794.

After Robespierre's fall in July 1794 the surviving revolutionaries built a republic designed to be un-radicalizable, the Directory, and spent five years defending it from both royalists and Jacobins. A young artillery officer named Bonaparte cleared a royalist rising off the Paris streets in Vendémiaire 1795, then made his name in Italy at bridges like Arcole in 1796. When the Directory's authority finally collapsed, it was Bonaparte who ended the Revolution he had risen through, seizing power in the coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799.
significance: More than any other event, the Revolution supplied modern politics with its vocabulary and its arguments. Left and right, nation and citizen, terror as a deliberate instrument of state, the idea that rights belong to people by virtue of being human rather than by grant of a king — all of it entered general circulation here, and was exported across Europe on the bayonets of French armies for the next twenty years. It also set the template for how revolutions are argued about ever since: whether emancipation justifies its body count, whether radical phases are betrayals of a moderate beginning or its logical conclusion, whether a revolution ends when a general takes over. Its own contradictions were exported too — a republic that proclaimed universal rights, abolished colonial slavery in 1794, and then saw Napoleon try to restore it in 1802.
coverage: Written from general reference accounts (Wikipedia, Britannica, World History Encyclopedia) plus the Roy Rosenzweig Center's primary-source archive; the ten dataset events skew toward Parisian journées and battles, so the countryside, the colonies, and the Revolution's institutional work — the assemblies, the legal and religious restructuring — are barely represented here. Casualty figures throughout are contested: the September Massacres and the Vendée in particular rest on incomplete records and on counts made by partisans of one side or the other, and the Vendée death toll remains a live political argument in France, not merely a scholarly one.

sources.title: Liberty, Equality, Fraternity: Exploring the French Revolution (Roy Rosenzweig Center for History and New Media / American Social History Project)
